commit.message:
app: nicknames were missing from the one policy people use most

Exchange keeps its own recipient list rather than using the shared SavedRecipients,
because it also renders destination tags. So when nicknames went into the shared
component they appeared on Spending limit and FXRP and not on Exchange — the policy
a tester named as the one they'd actually use.

Added there too. Swept the file afterwards for any address still rendered raw; the
only ones left are the input fields you type into and the copy buttons, which is
correct.

Where a nickname can be SET is now every list that shows saved addresses: Exchange,
Spending limit, FXRP payees. Scheduled and Conditional show a name if one exists but
have no list to click — their payee appears inline in a sentence.

fix: hooks were called after early returns — the account page crashed

Adding the spend-panel readiness check, I put useState and useEffect below the
`if (loading) return` guards. React requires the same hooks in the same order on
every render; on the loading pass those two never ran, so the component tore itself
down and the page showed "This page couldn't load".

Moved above every return, with the rule key derived inside the effect so it depends
only on state. Scanned the rest of the file for the same shape — clean.

How this got shipped is the part worth recording. eslint's react-hooks/rules-of-hooks
would have caught it immediately, and I ran eslint — but I'd been comparing problem
COUNTS against a baseline instead of reading the output, so a new error hid inside a
number I'd stopped looking at. tsc and next build both passed, and I reported "build
clean" as if that meant working. It doesn't: compiling says nothing about rendering.

Same class as the blank scheduled card a tester found. Both were UI changes verified
by compiling rather than by looking.

chore: gitignore content/ for launch copy

Marketing drafts were living in a session temp directory, which is neither backed up
nor permanent. They shouldn't be tracked either — outward-facing wording changes
constantly and reviewing it as code helps nobody. So: a real folder that git ignores.

Only the ignore rule is committed; the folder's contents stay local.

app: the rest of the form — including the question at the end of it

Cross-checking the feedback form against what shipped found four things I'd counted
as done and hadn't.

Nicknames were only on the exchange and spending-limit lists. They asked for four
policies; Scheduled and Conditional were missing, and Scheduled was worse than that
— it never showed WHO a line pays at all, only how much and how often. It does now,
by name where there is one.

The spending limit reads in the right order: the choice of who it can pay comes
before the list that choice produces, because you can't judge a list until you know
whether it's being consulted. The approved list now hides entirely under "Anyone",
which is stronger than the warning I added last time. "Max per payment" says what it
had never said — one cap across every recipient, not one each.

The Spend panel gets the better answer to their objection. They asked twice for it to
go from Scheduled and Conditional; deleting it would delete the payout, since on
Conditional that panel IS how a proven condition pays. So it now appears only when
the rule would actually permit something, and says why when it doesn't: "Nothing to
release yet" / "Nothing due yet".

And the question they closed with — "when a change is needed the only solution seems
to be to empty the wallet and create a new one, what countermeasures do you suggest?"
The countermeasure only exists before the lock, so that's where it belongs: arming
the lock now lists every destination the account will EVER be able to send to, and
says to make sure one of them is yours. It was asking people to confirm "forever"
without showing what forever contained.

app: actually remove the placeholder, not just stop writing it

The last change stopped inventing "Recovered account N" for future recoveries and
missed the obvious: anyone who had already recovered had the placeholder written into
localStorage as a real label. So the fix helped precisely the people who hadn't hit
the problem.

Strip it on read in lib/accounts.ts and write back once, so it's gone rather than
hidden — and so every consumer benefits at once. The account detail page was reading
the same label and would have kept showing it too; it now names an unlabelled account
by its policy, the same way the list does.

app: a recovered account should say what it is, not what number it is

Account labels are the one thing recovery genuinely can't get back — the contract has
no field for them and no event carries one, because you typed the name into a browser
and it stayed there. Putting them on-chain would fix that and shouldn't: labels say
things like "Binance deposit", and a public chain is a poor place to keep them
forever to save a rename.

But "Recovered account 3" was a bad answer to a question the chain can already
answer better. A recovered account now describes itself from what it actually is —
"Exchange & allowlist account", beside its own r-address, both read from chain state
we already fetch. Rename it if you like; it's recognisable either way.

app: name your addresses, and see when the allowance refills

The last two things the tester asked for.

Addresses can be named. Their point: several r-addresses across policies "without
recognisable names make it very confusing which wallet you're sending XRP to" — and
they're right that checking 34 characters of base58 by eye is not a thing to ask
before approving a payee. The name never replaces the address; both are on screen,
because showing only a nickname is a good way to approve the wrong one.

Nicknames live in localStorage, which we were just burned by — deliberately. A
nickname is the one kind of thing that can safely live there: losing it costs a
label, not an account, and a fresh browser degrades to exactly what the app showed
before they existed. The account list had to move on-chain because losing THAT looked
like losing money. Different stakes, different home.

And the spending limit now shows what a spending limit never told you: how much is
left, and when it refills. The contract knew both — only the config was ever surfaced,
never the spend against it. Reset times come from the same window arithmetic the rule
uses, so the countdown can't promise a refill the rule won't honour.

fxrp: the policy was a one-way street — give it an exit

A tester filed this as a suggestion; it was closer to a design flaw. An FXRP account
could mint, earn in a vault, exit the vault and redeem home — and then that XRP could
go nowhere, because every recipient except the Core Vault and the FSA wallet was
refused. Their words: "I can't ever sell, spend or transfer my FXRP, stXRP or XRP."
Value that can enter and never leave is a trap, not a guarantee.

The exit already existed in two halves. Redeem-home worked; paying the redeemed XRP
out did not. So FxrpRule gains an owner-approved payee list, exactly like the Exchange
policy, and only the second half was ever missing.

What deliberately does NOT change: FXRP itself still cannot be transferred to anyone.
Instruction 0x01 stays refused, so the way out remains redeem-home-then-pay — two
steps the rule can see and check. A test pins that approving a payee is not a back
door into the FXRP, because that is the guarantee worth keeping.

Same security posture as every other rule: an unlocked account trusts its control
key, and lock() freezes the payee list for good.

Deployed 0xAABAEA1D; the old rule is registered as superseded so the nine accounts on
it get the move prompt rather than silently losing their settings. 78/78, and proven
on-chain end to end: refused before approval, FXRP transfer-out still refused after
it, and 2 XRP settled to the approved address.

app: the rest of the tester's review, minus the two I disagreed with

Times. They scheduled a payment "for today", nothing had run by 07:50 UTC, and they
couldn't tell a wait from a failure — because every date was shown without the hour.
Runs land at 00:00 UTC and deadlines at 23:59 UTC, and neither said so anywhere.
Dates now carry the time in the reader's own zone, named, and the schedule field says
when runs land before anything is saved.

The Spend panel stays, renamed per policy. They asked for it to go, since it and
"Try to break it" looked like the same thing. But on Conditional that panel IS how
the payee gets paid once the condition is proven — deleting it would have deleted the
payout. On Scheduled it's the manual push for something already due. Both now say
that, instead of "Spend".

Spending limit, all as asked: "Already allowed" is now "Approved recipient list",
"Who's on the list?" is "Add approved recipients", the Add button no longer looks
secondary to Save, and the panel is split under "Who it can pay" / "How much it can
spend" so it's clear the allowance covers every payee.

And the trap they fell into: switching to "Anyone" leaves the approved addresses on
screen, which reads as still-in-force. It isn't. It now says so at the point of the
switch rather than leaving them to scroll up and infer it.

app: make the control key survivable

Four things a tester flagged, in the order they mattered.

Backing up is no longer optional or easy to miss. It stood at the bottom of the page,
which they said "can make it seem less important & be missed initially" — so it now
stands in front of account creation, and the only way past is to confirm you've
written it down. You can't own something worth losing before you've saved the thing
that protects it.

New keys are a twelve-word recovery phrase, not 64 hex characters — their point was
that hex is "difficult to write down - get this wrong & your assets are gone". The
phrase derives an identical account (verified), so nothing downstream changes, and
existing hex keys still load, export and import exactly as before.

The copy button is gone from the reveal. Their reasoning stands on its own: a
clipboard is the easiest place for this to leak from. That only became reasonable
advice once writing it down was realistic.

And it now says how it's generated — crypto.getRandomValues, in the browser, never
sent anywhere — because after the Coldcard business people are right to ask.

One correction to their review, and our fault for never saying it: losing the control
key is NOT loss of funds. pay() has no owner check, so an account keeps obeying its
rules and can still pay anyone those rules already allow. What's lost is the ability
to CHANGE the rules. Both the gate and the reveal now say so.

app: a control key finds its own accounts on any browser

Tester feedback, and the blocker they said would stop them using it: importing the
control key into another browser session brings the key but not the accounts. The
key import worked fine — the account list lives in localStorage, so a fresh browser
showed nothing, which reads as "my funds are gone".

They aren't, and never were: WalletCreated indexes `owner`, so the list is derivable
from the key alone. /api/accounts-of does that, and the accounts page folds anything
missing into what the browser already knew. lib/accounts.ts predicted this exact fix
in a comment and it stayed a TODO until someone hit it.

Verified: the deployer key recovers all 14 of its accounts from the chain, and an
address that never created one gets an empty list rather than everyone's.

Labels and salts stay local — neither is needed to use an account — so recovered
ones arrive named "Recovered account N" and can be renamed. Server-side because the
public RPC caps getLogs at 30 blocks, same as the other read routes.

links: make every settled thing checkable, including the FDC half

Recent payments listed an amount and a destination and dropped the hash, so the
account's own history was the one part you had to take on trust. Every row now links
to the ledger. That panel is shared, so it covers all five policies at once.

The FDC transactions were worse off: the attestation request was captured and never
printed at all, so the logs showed a release without showing that a voting round had
been asked for, paid for and waited on — the half that makes it an attestation rather
than an assertion. Both watchers now log it, and the single-shot release path links
its transaction too.

And a proven condition now says how it was proven: the account page shows the Flare
voting round and links the transaction that carried the proof. "Proven ✓" is a claim;
the round number and the tx are where someone checks it.

executors + app: link every completed action to the explorer

The watcher logged a bare hash — which is the right information in the least useful
form, since verifying it meant copying it somewhere. All three watchers now log the
full Coston2 explorer URL, which Railway renders as a link, so a payment is one click
from being checked rather than taken on trust.

Same gap in the app: the FXRP actions produce a transaction and never showed it. The
progress tracker now carries the hash from write() and links it, so the thing you're
waiting on is verifiable while you wait — not just after the balance moves. The spend
panel already did this for its XRPL payment; this brings mint, put-to-work, exit and
claim in line.

Worth noting which chain each link points at, because they answer different
questions: the Flare transaction is the AUTHORISATION — the rule agreeing — while
the XRPL transaction is the money moving. For a page whose argument is that the
contract decides, the authorisation is the one worth showing.

executor: print who you are and what you can afford, on every boot

Your scheduled payment came due at 00:00 UTC and the watcher couldn't send it: the
executor key had run out of C2FLR. The error names the problem — "the total cost of
executing this transaction exceeds the balance of the account" — but never prints
WHICH account, so there was nothing to go and top up.

Now every watcher logs its executor address and balance at startup, and warns below
1 C2FLR with the faucet URL. A silent countdown becomes something you can see, and
the warning arrives long before the first missed payment instead of after it.

Nothing was lost, which is the design working: authorize() is reached through pay(),
and the transaction never left the machine — so the schedule didn't advance. Still
5 runs left, still due, and it retries every 60s once there's gas.

Also records the claim encoding as verified: 0x13 with the period in the value
field moved 10 FXRP back to liquid and flipped isWithdrawClaimed. The vault exit is
now proven end to end — deposit, exit, wait out the period, claim.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

app: tell people what they can spend before they spend it

Every amount field drew on a balance the user can't be expected to hold in their
head — XRP on the ledger for a mint, liquid FXRP for a deposit, whole lots for a
redemption — and validated on submit. So the sequence was: type 100, press the
button, get told 100 was never possible.

The balances now sit in state rather than being fetched at click time, so each field
says what it has while you type, offers "use max", turns red when the number is too
big, and disables the action rather than letting it fail. Mint, put-to-work, bring-
home, and the one-off send panel all read the same way.

Two things the fields now know that the user otherwise had to: XRPL keeps ~1 XRP as
an unspendable base reserve, so it is never part of a mintable or sendable balance;
and redemption is in whole 10 FXRP lots, so "you have 19.775 FXRP" is really "one
lot available" — and below one lot the button says so instead of failing.

fxrp: build the vault exit — it never needed event indexing

The code said withdrawals were view-only because "claim params aren't readable
on-chain". Reading FirelightVault shows otherwise: withdrawalsOf(period, account)
and isWithdrawClaimed are both public views, so a small scan of periods around the
current one finds every pending exit. No indexer, no stored state, and it survives a
refresh or a different device.

What the mechanism actually is, measured on Coston2 today. A redeem burns your
shares immediately and files the claim under the NEXT period; claimWithdraw then
requires that period to have ENDED. Periods are 4 hours, so a redeem at 17:43 was
filed under period 84 and unlocks at 21:52 — the money is genuinely unreachable for
up to two period lengths, which nothing in the FSA interface tells you.

So the UI says it: "Take it out" on a position, then an "On its way out" list with
the real unlock time and a Collect button that stays disabled until it's true.
Upshift is left out rather than half-built — its exit path is a different shape and
I haven't verified it.

NOT YET VERIFIED: the claim instruction encoding (0x13 with the period as the
reference value). It's the natural encoding and mirrors deposit/exit, but period 84
doesn't end until 21:52 UTC so it cannot be exercised before then. Everything up to
the claim is proven live.

fxrp: stop the progress tracker claiming success before the money moves

Tracing the token transfers corrected something I'd assumed. The vault deposit is
ATOMIC — at T+198s, 10 FXRP left and 10 vault shares arrived in the same second. The
FXRP is never in limbo, so there was no "in transit" state to build. It is simply
liquid until the instant it isn't.

The real problem was the tracker. Its give-up timer flipped done:true after 180s
regardless of what happened — and a deposit takes 198s, so it reported success
eighteen seconds before the deposit occurred. A timer running out is not evidence
the money moved. It now says "still working, longer than usual, but nothing is
lost", and only the balance actually changing marks it done.

The countdown is also per action now, because they differ more than one number can
cover: mint 129s, deposit 198s, redeem 112s measured. A single 90s countdown expired
mid-wait on all three, which reads as failure.

And it says the true, reassuring thing during the wait: your balance won't change
until this lands, the whole move happens in one transaction at the end, nothing has
left your account yet. Three minutes of an unchanged balance otherwise reads as a
click that didn't work.

fxrp: tell people what they'll receive, and how long it really takes

Measured the whole round trip on a fresh account rather than estimating it:

  mint            129s   50 XRP -> 49.775 FXRP
  vault deposit  ~200s   10 FXRP into Firelight
  bring home      112s   20 FXRP -> 19.9 XRP

Two things that measurement exposed, neither of them speed.

The mint fee was never disclosed. 50 XRP became 49.775 FXRP and the word "fee"
appeared nowhere in the panel — a user deposits 50, receives less, and has to work
out why from a balance. FAssets keeps max(0.25%, 0.1 FXRP) plus a 0.1 FXRP fee to
whoever completes the mint; the panel now reads all three from the AssetManager and
says what will arrive before you commit, including refusing amounts smaller than the
fee. Read live so it stays true if Flare retunes it.

And the progress tracker counted down from 90s against a trip that takes 129s, so it
hit zero mid-wait — which reads as a failure rather than a wait. Now 150s, and the
copy says "about two minutes" instead of "~1-2 min".

Not doing the latency work I proposed: a Flare bot completed the mint, not our
executor, so our poll intervals aren't in the critical path and tuning them buys
nothing. Our watcher stays as the fallback for when their bots don't act.

docs: write down the destination-tag finding before we forget why we're safe

Reading MemoInstructionsFacet after Flare's custom-instructions announcement turned
up a warning we appear to violate: XRPL payments to smart accounts must not carry a
destination tag, and our enclave derives one from the top 4 bytes of the payment
reference. For an FXRP mint those bytes are the FAssets DIRECT_MINTING prefix, so
every mint goes out tagged 1178751058.

It matters because DirectMintingFacet._decodeTarget lets a registered tag win
outright and never reads the memo — the memo being the thing FxrpRule pins so a
stolen control key can't repoint a mint. One tag registration would capture every
Keyless mint.

It isn't reachable: MintingTagManager allocates tags sequentially from a counter
currently at 338, so the cheapest of our tags is 33.5 million reservations away at
100 C2FLR each. Every figure re-checked on-chain before committing.

So this is a dependency, not a bug — and the dependency is on someone else's
implementation detail. If Flare ever allows reserving a chosen tag, we're vulnerable
that day with no change on our side and no signal. That's worth a file rather than a
memory.

Also records why we're not fixing it now: the fix is in the enclave, /go/** is a
Railway watch path, and restarting the sim enclave loses every account's key. The
prerequisite is threshold key backup, which mainnet needs anyway.

Two smaller entries alongside it: authorize() advancing before the enclave submits,
and the superseded-rule migration checklist.
But this will be researched on and fixed before mainnet

app: show dollars, keep enforcing XRP

Amounts are denominated and enforced in XRP on purpose. A cap's whole job is to be
an absolute bound, and a bound that moves with the market isn't one — denominate in
dollars and a falling price lets more XRP leave for the same "limit", so the worst
case stops being statable at all. That matters most exactly where it's tempting: on
a locked account, runs x amount is the only thing bounding total outflow.

But people think in dollars. So the conversion lives at the very edge — a display
hint beside a number the contract already fixed, from a route that touches nothing
else. If the price source is down the hint simply doesn't render and the panel is
what it was before.

Shown on the scheduled panel (next payment, each line, the composer preview) and
beside a spending allowance.

Caveat: Coinbase isn't reachable from my sandbox, so the live rate is unverified
from here — only the failure path is, which renders nothing. Worth an eyeball in
the browser.

The general rule this follows: anything that softens a guarantee belongs in the
interface, never in the rule.

app: an account left on a replaced rule should say so

I redeployed ScheduledRule twice in two days — once to make every schedule finite,
once to add month-end payments — and stranded three accounts on the older versions.
The UI handled it badly. The list called them "custom policy"; the account page
found no matching rule key and fell through to "This account has no policy yet, so
it can't spend", which is alarming and untrue. The account has a policy. Its money
is fine. It's on a version nothing watches any more.

SUPERSEDED_RULES names those deployments, and a stranded account now explains itself
and offers the move as one transaction — with the part that isn't automatic stated
plainly: settings live in the rule, so the schedule has to be set up again.

Worse, and separate: scheduled.mjs still defaulted SCHEDULED_RULE to the address it
replaced. Railway only has WATCHER and EXECUTOR_KEY set, so the live watcher has
been polling a contract nobody uses. No schedule was missed — none was due — but it
would have been, silently, on 31 August.

scheduled: show when a schedule ends, not how many times it runs

Prompted by a fair question: what if someone enters 13? Nothing — but 4,000,000,000
is equally accepted, and that is the endless standing order I claimed to have made
unreachable, wearing a number. The rule does guarantee every schedule terminates.
It does not guarantee it terminates in your lifetime, and it was the second promise
the UI was making when it said "12 payments left, then it stops — so locking this
account is safe".

A count can't be judged on sight: 12 is a year, 4 billion is longer than the sun
has, and both look reasonable typed into a box. So every place that showed a bare
count now shows the date the last payment lands — composer preview, the account
notice, and the can/can't card.

Past a century, scheduleEnd returns null rather than a date (large counts overflow
the date range outright), and the UI stops claiming locking is safe: "far enough out
that this schedule never realistically ends — don't lock this account."

No contract change. The guarantee was fine; the sentence describing it wasn't.

scheduled: pay on the last day of the month

The date picker stopped at the 28th so a schedule could never land on a day that
doesn't exist in February — correct, but it ruled out month-end payroll, which is
how a lot of companies actually pay. No fixed date expresses "the last day": the
31st is missing from April, and the 28th is only month end in a non-leap February.

CalendarLib gains a LAST_DAY sentinel, resolved as the day before the next month
starts — so leap years and 30/31-day months need no table and no special cases. In
the UI it's one more option in the same dropdown, "the last day", and the sentence
preview reads it back as "on the last day of every month".

Tests walk a real year: 28 Feb 2027, then 31 March, then 30 April; 29 February in
leap 2028; and 31 December rolling into 31 January. Two of those failed first on my
own wrong constants, not the contract — worth saying, since the calendar is exactly
where a plausible-looking expectation slips through.

Redeployed to 0x683bDB59; the demo account now pays at month end, 31 August next.
73/73, and the UI's preview date agrees with the chain to the second.

scheduled: make the composer readable, and stop it accepting nonsense

Five controls in a wrapping row broke into ragged lines, and "how many times"
orphaned itself under a field it has nothing to do with. Fixed grid instead, so
the layout is the same every time regardless of which fields a unit shows.

Labels now say what they mean: "How much, each time?" with the exact-amount promise
in the hint, "How many payments?" with "then it stops for good", "Start from" with
"leave blank to start with the next one". The month-day picker explains why it ends
at the 28th rather than just stopping there.

Each line reads itself back as a sentence — "25 XRP to rNayb… on the 1st of every
month, 12 times — first on 1 September 2026" — because four individually correct
fields still don't tell you what you just agreed to. The date comes from a mirror of
CalendarLib.nextBoundaryAfter, checked against the deployed rule: monthly, weekly,
daily, offset and start-date cases all agree with the chain.

Save was clickable with the form empty and failed at the alert. It's now gated, and
says what's outstanding instead of what went wrong.

app: scheduled accounts were invisible to the account page

Pre-submission QA found the gap. CapabilityCard — the "what this account can &
can't do" card, the whole block moment — had no branch for the scheduled rule, so
a payroll account showed an empty Can column. /api/rule-config didn't know the rule
either and returned the conditional shape, and because `configured` fell through to
false, a scheduled account could never be locked. One missing case, three symptoms.

The API now replays LineAdded, using ScheduleConfigured as the delimiter: configure()
deletes and re-pushes every line, so the current schedule is the set sharing the
latest configure's transaction. Without that, a replaced schedule would list its old
lines beside its new ones — verified against an account whose 500 XRP line was
replaced by a 25 XRP one, which now reports only the 25.

The card says what the policy actually promises: pays exactly this, on this day,
this many times; can't pay a penny more or less, can't pay early, can't pay anyone
else.

scheduled: let a schedule start later, and fund the demos

startAt was in the ABI and always sent as 0, so every schedule began at the next
boundary and nobody could say "start in January". The composer now takes a date;
blank still means the next one. The rule snaps whatever you pick forward to the
next matching slot, so choosing the 3rd on a monthly line still lands on the 1st
and the schedule stays calendar-true.

The four /see demo accounts held no XRP, so their explorer links — the ones the
page invites you to click — went somewhere empty. Funded from the testnet faucet.

That left the scheduled demo owing 500 XRP a month against a 100 XRP balance,
permanently underfunded and unable to ever demonstrate the thing it describes.
Resized to 25 XRP, so when the watcher wakes on 1 September it will make a real
payment on the ledger rather than log a skip.

Verified on-chain: a mid-January start on a monthly line is accepted, a date in
the past reverts with "start date is in the past".

env: stop handing new clones a dead diamond

.env.example still pointed FLARE_TEE_MANAGER at 0x004224fa — the manager Flare
replaced in July. It isn't obviously broken: it still has code and still answers,
it just doesn't know extension 65645, so it returns the zero address and every
instruction quietly goes nowhere. That reads as a bug in your own contract, which
is a long way to travel for a stale variable.

Same class of thing bit me this week: a stale ESCROW_RULE in a local .env sent me
debugging a rule that was fine. So the file now carries every live address —
manager, accounts, all five rules, the FSA diamond — each verified on-chain before
committing, plus the retired deployments listed as retired. The old FdcEscrowRule
is called out explicitly: it's still deployed, and it could be released by an
attestation of any API returning the same value.

Secrets stay placeholders; .env remains gitignored.

executor: make the scheduled watcher deployable

Registers watch:scheduled and a `due` dry-run in package.json, and adds a
railway.json so a watcher service redeploys when a watcher changes — and not when
the frontend or the enclave does. The enclave keeps its own narrower watchPatterns
for the reason it always had: a restart costs the sim enclave its keys.

Also fixes a shutdown bug the smoke test exposed. start.mjs exited 1 on any signal,
including SIGTERM — which is exactly how Railway stops a service on redeploy. With
the ON_FAILURE restart policy this file now sets, every ordinary deploy would have
looked like a crash and invited a restart loop. A shutdown we asked for exits 0;
anything else still reports honestly so the platform brings the watcher back.

Verified by running the real entrypoint: starts, polls the deployed rule, stops
clean.

scheduled: something has to actually run the standing order

The rule enforced a schedule but nothing executed it, so a payment came due and sat
there until a human pushed it through the send form. The pitch is that you never
sign the weekly transaction; you were still signing it.

scheduled.mjs watches every account on the rule and runs each line the moment it
falls due. It resolves payees by replaying LineAdded — the rule stores only
keccak(recipient), so the events are the only way to learn who to pay, and there is
no registry to keep in sync.

It reads the XRP balance before attempting anything. authorize() advances nextDue
before the enclave submits, so paying from an account that can't cover it converts a
fundable payment into a permanently missed one; the ledger's 1 XRP base reserve is
excluded because it can never be spent. When the ledger can't be reached it skips
the tick rather than guessing.

Also: the landing page listed four policies while the app offered five, and its
how-it-works copy still named "a subscription" — a rule retired months ago.

Verified live: payee resolution recovers rNayb1… from a stored hash; the balance
guard correctly skips an unfunded account, an account holding 22 XRP against a 500
XRP run, and an unreadable one.

see: say which account you're breaking

The page invited people to try to break an account without ever naming it — no
address, nothing to copy, nothing to look up. "Try to break it" is a weaker claim
when the thing being broken is anonymous.

Each demo now shows its real XRPL address: copyable, and linked to the ledger

conditional: ConditionalRule v2 — fixes a critical forged-proof vulnerability

Rebuilds the FDC "pay when the world proves it" policy. The superseded
FdcEscrowRule had three defects, all verified against Coston2:

1. It could never release. It called `verifyJsonApi`, which does not exist on the
   live FdcVerification — the function is `verifyWeb2Json`. Every release()
   reverted. (Interface corrected.)
2. Its committed hash could never match: the UI hashed free text while the
   contract compared keccak(abiEncodedData). Structurally unsatisfiable.
3. CRITICAL: anyone could release anyone's escrow. It verified the proof was
   genuine and that the RESPONSE matched, but never which request produced it.
   Conditions are naturally a jq predicate returning a bool, so every boolean
   escrow committed to the same hash — keccak(abi.encode(true)) = 0xb10e2d5276…
   — and release() is permissionless. Demonstrated live: an attestation of
   "github stars > 0" yields exactly that hash, so it would have released a
   "delivery == true" escrow.

ConditionalRule pins the WHOLE request — keccak(abi.encode(requestBody)) covers
url, method, headers, queryParams, body, jq and abi signature — so only an
attestation of that exact request returning that exact value can release it.
Binding the whole struct also closes the same-url/different-query hole (CoinGecko
/simple/price ids=ripple vs ids=bitcoin). `requestHashOf()` lets clients ask the
contract for the commitment instead of re-implementing ABI encoding.

while INIT always worked. Root cause found in tee-proxy source, and it was never
latency: pkg/instruction/meta/meta.go resolves an instruction's cosigners by
switching on the opCommand ALONE, ignoring opType:

    switch data.OPCommand {
    case op.Pay.Hash(), op.Reissue.Hash():   // our KEYLESS_XRP/"PAY" landed here
        xrpCosigners(...)                    // -> ParsePaymentInstruction(data)
    default:                                 // <- what we need (INIT hit this)

treat our instruction as a Flare PMW payment and decode our XrplPayment as

into go array"), so startVoteBox errors, no vote box is created, the instruction
never reaches consensus, and it is never delivered. A custom opType does not
protect you: sendInstructions validates the (Type,Command) pair, but the proxy's
cosigner switch only looks at Command.

drive our own TEE machines instead of TeePayments, which we cannot use.

- AuthorizedPayPolicy: _authorizedPay now calls FlareTeeManager.sendInstructions
  with a custom opType (system opTypes are reserved for extension 0). The policy
  contract is the extension's instructionsSender, so the enclave holding the XRPL
  key takes orders from it and from nothing else.
- KeylessRedemptionPolicy: add a redemptionPaid guard. The AssetManager only
  reverts once a payment is CONFIRMED, which is minutes after we authorize it;
  until then the request is still ACTIVE, so a permissionless payRedemption could
  otherwise be called repeatedly and drain the agent's reserve.
- KeylessDemoPolicy: drop reissue(). It took caller-supplied payment details and
  never re-ran _checkPolicy, which was a hole straight through the policy. Retries
  belong to the enclave, which re-derives fields from the authorized instruction.
- Delete ITeePayments/PMWTypes (their signatures did not match the deployed ABI
  anyway) and the stale derisk script.
- Tests: 11 passing, incl. double-pay and "no instruction reaches the enclave"
  on the adversary path.

Pivot to own FCE extension; add bootstrap script

The PMW design cannot work: TeePayments.addPMWMultisigAccount requires the
wallet's project to sit on extension id 0 (the system extension, owned by
Flare governance), so a third-party contract can never become a PMW account's
authorization address. Verified live on Coston2 — a cold EOA calling
createProject(0, ...) reverts OwnerNotAllowed().

Running our own TEE extension IS permissionless, so take that path instead:

- IFlareTeeManager: the FlareTeeManager diamond surface we drive.
- BootstrapExtension.s.sol: register the extension, self-allow as machine and
  project owner, declare the XRP key type, and register the TEE code hash.
  Dry-runs clean against live Coston2 (would claim extension 454).
- BindPolicy: rebind the extension so the policy contract is the only address
  its TEE machines will obey.
- foundry.toml: paris -> shanghai. Flare's deployed contracts use PUSH0, which
  paris predates, so fork simulation failed with EvmError: NotActivated.
- Untrack docs/ (internal research notes).
